extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity, academics, and the general public following cases of scientific misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Judging public presentations or apology talks given by researchers found guilty of misconduct — whether they adequately explain, apologize, and address harms. Includes considerations of speaker selection and institutional responses to fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content about the wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: The talk should get down to the roots of what was done and explain the reasons and steps that led to the misconduct. A mere admission followed by colourful language that keeps faults at arm's length is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters criticized the TEDx talk for admitting fraud but then offering only colourful language and external attributions (e.g., 'lost his moral compass'), rather than detailing why the fabrication happened. Anti-pattern: glossing over causes or offering facile psychological labels (e.g., 'goal obsession') without concrete explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine remorse and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker should demonstrate honest regret and take responsibility, not appear primarily concerned with reputation or attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comments ask whether Stapel is 'sorry for what he did or for having been caught' and note a lack of 'deep self searching nor honest regret.' Anti-patterns include self-justifying language, trivializing the misconduct, or framing the talk as a comeback/PR tour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address harm to victims and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper apology/talk about misconduct should acknowledge and address the consequences for co-authors, students, colleagues, and others whose careers or reputations were damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters observed the speech focused on Stapel himself and 'not about the consequences of his actions for other people whose careers were damaged.' Guidance: explicitly name harms, express sorrow for those affected, and outline steps taken or proposed to repair damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the stepwise process of misconduct (instructional value)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be useful to the community, the talk should document the small steps and personal/situational processes that led to large-scale fabrication, so others can learn and prevent similar cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One comment lamented lack of 'small steps leading to the personal justification of data fabrication' and said documenting that process would let the community profit. Example guidance: map decisions, pressures, and institutional incentives that enabled misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker selection — credibility and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is scientific fraud, consider whether the speaker is the best messenger; a researcher who has studied misconduct may be more appropriate than the perpetrator seeking attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters argued TEDx should have invited 'a respectable researcher who actually studied the phenomenon' rather than an 'attention-seeking fraudster.' Organizers should weigh educational value and ethics of platforming someone who may benefit from notoriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding notoriety / platforming as rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers should avoid giving prominent platforms to individuals whose appearance primarily serves their publicity or rehabilitation rather than community benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note Stapel's book tour, theatre tour, and public appearances and question whether the talk 'rewards a Retraction leaderboard member.' Anti-pattern: treating a fraudster appearance as a publicity opportunity without clear restorative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional openness and balanced handling of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A preferable institutional response to fraud is open, balanced discussion and transparency rather than cover-up or overly punitive approaches that hide systemic problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter contrasted Dutch openness with perceived US/UK tendencies toward cover-up for powerful individuals and heavy punishment for junior offenders; observed that a measured, open response 'in the long run has to be better than the head-in-the-sand approach.' Guidance: encourage transparent inquiry and proportionate, systemic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format suitability for depth (venue and audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a venue and format appropriate to the complexity of the subject; short prepared talks or casual Q&A (e.g., on a train) may not allow deep exploration of root causes and reparative actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters questioned whether a 17-minute TEDx talk on a train with limited Q&A can sufficiently explore extensive fraud and its consequences. Guidance: for complex misconduct cases, prefer longer formats, panels, or expert-moderated discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete reparative actions and restitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond apology, the speaker (or institution) should outline concrete steps taken or proposed to repair harms — e.g., correcting the scientific record, compensating or supporting affected trainees, returning ill-gotten gains where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several comments asked why there was no mention of making effort to 'repair some of the harm' or returning titles/funds. Guidance: identify tangible remedial measures and timelines; absence of such plans is a sign of a weak apology.
